g.text: Correctness here is not a lock that is fast enough - it is an operation that was never order-dependent
Two components in this design are not 'compute a hash' or 'store a row': the metric aggregator, and the gate between a p-value existing and being allowed to mean anything.
Interfaces, and what each one deliberately does not know
ExperimentAnalyzer - the orchestrator, implementing none of the above
A binary metric (did the user convert) uses the z-test for proportions; a
continuous one (revenue per user) uses Welch's t-test, which does NOT assume the
two variants have equal variance. Both sit behind one interface, so the analyzer
never knows which is running - and a future sequential test drops in without
The analyzer depends on all of them plus a PeekingGate, and implements none of the
storage, hashing or statistics itself. Which is what makes the extension
questions answerable: the interfaces already say which component should own each
new piece of behaviour, before you have worked out what the behaviour does.
Assignment is a pure function over a FROZEN definition
for variant in experimentDef.variants: # ordered, FROZEN at start
The per-experiment SALT is what keeps one user's bucketing independent across
different experiments. Without it, hash(experimentId + userId) for two
experiments with similar id structure could correlate more than chance alone
would explain - and correlated assignment across experiments quietly invalidates
The variants and their bucket ranges come from the snapshot taken when the
experiment STARTED. This function never consults a live, editable config - the
same reason a feature flag's evaluator never re-derives its rollout math from a
Two partitions, no shared state, and one associative formula
One user's exposure and conversion always land on the SAME partition, because the stream is sharded by user_id. Each partition
maintains its own triple with NO VISIBILITY INTO ANY OTHER PARTITION'S STATE AT ALL - and never retains a raw value, which is
what makes a per-variant mean and variance computable without storing every observation.
in, or how many merge at
The one piece of code between 'a p-value exists' and 'a p-value is allowed to mean anything'
note: 'not a final read; do not act on this' }
return { status: 'final', pValue: r.pValue, confidenceInterval: r.ci }
analyze() can be called as often as anyone likes - a dashboard hitting it once a
minute causes no statistical harm - because the function itself REFUSES to hand
back a 'final' verdict until the pre-registered sample size or duration has
Everything before that point is explicitly labelled 'monitoring_only': visible
for trend-watching, and STRUCTURALLY INCAPABLE of being read as 'significant,
ship it'. That is the peeking discipline enforced in code rather than left as a
And note the ordering: SRM is checked BEFORE the significance test, and a flagged
SRM returns 'untrustworthy' INSTEAD OF a p-value - not alongside one. A skewed
split means control and treatment likely differ in ways beyond the treatment
itself, so reporting a p-value over a broken comparison is worse than reporting
Three error cases designed for deliberately
an exposure event claims a variant the hash does not agree with
never trust the variant a client-supplied exposure event carries. assign() is recomputed SERVER-SIDE from (experimentId,
userId) and compared against the logged variant before the exposure is accepted. A mismatch - a stale client cache, a
tampered request - is dropped rather than silently corrupting a variant's summary with a user who was never assigned to it.
a conversion arrives after its attribution window closed
neither silently dropping it nor silently folding it into an already-computed summary is acceptable, so it is routed to a
distinct 'late, unattributed' record - the same instinct as a late-arriving ad click, against a window measured in days
not a warning alongside the results: analyze() returns 'untrustworthy' and no p-value at all.
The one place a real ordering guarantee matters
read mean at t1 -> computed over 4,813 observations
-> the gate opens on a MIX of two different sample sizes
committedHorizonReached() has to read a CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT of (n, mean,
variance). Reading n from one moment and mean from a slightly later one - after
another event has already been ingested - could let the gate open on a mixture
that never existed as a single state.
the aggregator publishes each triple as ONE atomic reference swap
So any reader - including the gate - always sees one fully-consistent triple,
never a partially-updated one. The same immutable-snapshot technique the
feature-flag design uses for its config swap: never mutate what a reader might
already be holding; publish a new whole object instead.
Strategy SignificanceTest - z-test for a binary metric, Welch's t-test for a continuous one, and a future
sequential test, all interchangeable behind one interface
Immutable snapshot the aggregator's atomic reference swap for its per-variant triples
Repository MetricAggregator and SrmChecker hide their storage and their math; the analyzer touches neither a
Guard clause / gate committedHorizonReached() is a single NAMED checkpoint that every path to a 'final' verdict has to
pass through - rather than a discipline every caller has to remember on their own
